title: ATM withdrawals are just buying paper at a markup: how the machines became payment networks
dek: ATMs aren't fundamentally about cash withdrawal—they're about paying for paper. The companies running them unexpectedly discovered they actually controlled a payment rail, far more profitable than selling paper.
why: The first half explains a system everyone uses daily but nobody thinks about—ATMs and the debit-card network behind them. The second half is a social observation about the decline of bank tellers as a profession. Both parts reward listening.
who: People working in payments infrastructure or banking chains, and anyone curious why bank tellers are rapidly disappearing as a profession.
skip: The opening analogy about Black Friday stockpiling and AWS legends can be skipped without losing the main thread.

points.h: Cross-bank networks were necessary to solve the ATM fragmentation problem
points.body: Initially, every ATM operator negotiated separately with each bank—a machine might work with only a handful of banks, depending on individual deals. This was inefficient for all three parties: banks didn't want to negotiate with operators who had only ten machines; operators wanted access to all customers, not a subset; customers didn't want to search the city for a machine that accepted their card. When Cirrus emerged as a cross-bank network, starting as an alliance of six banks, it solved all three problems. After Mastercard acquired Cirrus for $40 million, operators only needed one negotiation to access many banks' customers, and the network charged operators per transaction.

points.h: Settlement delays expose the capital-intensive nature of ATM operations
points.body: When you stand at an ATM, a series of hedging transactions happens: the network arranges for your bank to owe the network money instead of owing you, while simultaneously arranging for the bank to owe the ATM operator. The operator releases cash. But settlement is much slower than the transaction itself—the network gets paid by your bank the next day, while the operator often waits days for the network, usually through slow channels like ACH. The capital pressure in running ATMs isn't the machines (which cost a few thousand dollars each), but carrying inventory of this 'magical paper' and financing the unfinished transactions.

points.h: ATM networks and payment rails are actually the same thing
points.body: Because ATM networks already possessed all the structural features of a payment rail, they moved into payment processing—transactions that have nothing to do with physical cash or paper at all. Running a payment rail is a far better business than selling paper, even marked-up paper. This is why checkout asks 'debit or credit?'—it's really asking which rail to send your transaction through, the credit-card rail or the debit-card rail. Most cashiers asked this question have no idea what it means.

points.h: Durbin Amendment created invisible payment networks nobody has heard of
points.body: The 2010 Durbin Amendment required every debit card to run on at least two unaffiliated networks, with merchants able to choose which one. The credit-card networks each count as one; the remaining slot filled by networks like STAR and Accel—debit networks born from ATM infrastructure, unaffiliated with Visa or Mastercard. These alternatives charge far lower fees than the major brands, but almost no consumers know they exist, and few merchants have the capacity or data to truly optimize which rail to use.

points.h: Supermarkets asking for cash back are cutting their own costs
points.body: Large merchants pay banks to deposit cash—roughly three basis points per $10,000 for large operators, similar for small businesses. Having customers pull cash directly at the register instead of depositing it into the bank, then having customers withdraw it, eliminates this fee entirely. It also moves money into the merchant's account faster, earning interest sooner, faster than physically transporting cash to the bank.

points.h: Japanese wage structures force ATMs to stockpile vastly more cash
points.body: Japan's government and financial institutions push for cashlessness, but most of the country's employers pay salaries on a tightly concentrated day: the 25th of each month. Many households withdraw most of their salary in cash that same day. To handle this predictable surge, Japanese ATMs typically stockpile cash—hundreds of thousands of dollars—before the 25th. This inventory runs 50 to 100 times larger than the typical daily holding in comparable American machines.

points.h: Branch managers were once community intelligence officers, now they're just clerks
points.body: In the 1970s, the branch manager was the bank's presence in the community, drawing on an informal intelligence network of tellers to understand which businesses were struggling, who shouldn't get more credit. They made real lending decisions based on this. Today, branch staffs are systematically deskilled: routine decisions go to headquarters computers and remote decision-makers. Managers no longer make meaningful credit judgments, and even operational decisions—like whether to expedite a check—have been optimized away. Tellers have lost even more power than their managers.

points.h: Teller turnover exceeds 20 percent annually; it is no longer a career
points.body: Teller work is heavily scripted—employees input what the computer tells them, while also being saddled with sales targets that career tellers don't typically have commission structures for. Meanwhile, AML and KYC rules have tightened; tellers are now first-line intelligence analysts expected to report suspicious transactions, putting them at odds with the customers they serve. As higher-paid alternatives like dental hygienists emerge—requiring similar education but paying 2.4 times as much—the pool of potential tellers gets siphoned away, leaving behind workers stripped of skill. The industry now needs to recruit roughly 25,000 new tellers annually just to replace turnover.

quotes.text: The typical transaction rhymes with "I'll sell you $40 worth of paper for $43, with a few minutes of operator attention being required every several hundred transactions."
Operating payment rails is a much, much better business than selling paper, even at eye-popping markups.

That's right: the ATM networks long since realized that, since they necessarily have all the features of a payment rail, they should get into the payments business even if it was disconnected from the machines they are most associated with and even if no paper was involved.
99.98% of people who read a newsletter or listen to a podcast specifically about financial infrastructure probably had no idea this option existed.
